https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4539.text: During its presidency of the Three Seas Initiative, Slovakia wants to closely cooperate with Poland on further developing regional cooperation and advancing priority infrastructure projects, said Foreign Affairs Ministry's State Secretary Rastislav Chovanec, who received a Polish delegation led by deputy director of the Polish Foreign Affairs Ministry's Economic Section Sebastian Barkowski on Tuesday (21 July). "Poland, as the largest and founding member of the Three Seas Initiative, is striving to raise awareness of its importance, while it is essential for Slovakia to take into account the interests of individual participating countries. During our current presidency, which will culminate with the presidential summit and business forum in Bratislava in April 2027, we are keen to work closely and exchange experience with our Polish partners," said the state secretary. At the same time, both sides agreed that cooperation within the Three Seas Initiative must be based on sound economic principles and the principle of return on investment, while it must create opportunities to increase investment in the participating countries and help reduce regional disparities between them. The talks also followed up on the conclusions of the Three Seas Initiative presidential summit held in April in Dubrovnik, Croatia. The partners discussed the priorities of Slovakia's leadership, focusing in particular on the further development of infrastructure projects in the areas of transport, energy and digitalisation, as well as on fostering innovation. The State Secretary also highlighted Slovakia's strengths in advanced industries and confirmed the country's interest in developing bilateral cooperation in innovative sectors. "Slovakia has a high-quality talent pool in emerging digital technologies and artificial intelligence. We would like to deepen our dialogue with Poland in these areas," said Chovanec. The Three Seas Initiative was established in 2016 and brings together 13 EU countries. Its aim is to strengthen cooperation and support the development of macro-regional projects in the area of energy, transport and digital connectivity along the north–south corridor between the Baltic, Adriatic and Black Sea. Source: TASR

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Freight in front of a Ukrainian Antonov plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport after a drone was spotted nearby. Photograph: NEWS5/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Freight in front of a Ukrainian Antonov plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport after a drone was spotted nearby. Photograph: NEWS5/AFP/Getty Images Russia Analysis Europe calls out Russia’s ‘hybrid war’ in public. But how can it make Putin pay? Pjotr Sauer Governments are now quicker to point the finger at Moscow, but critics say their inaction invites more sabotage Fri 4 Sep 2026 01.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 4 Sep 2026 05.55 EDT Share Russia’s suspected sabotage campaign across Europe appears to be gathering pace again, confronting governments with a problem they have struggled to solve since the start of the war in Ukraine: how to impose a meaningful cost on Moscow for attacks that remain deliberately below the threshold of conventional war. Over the past month alone, an explosives-laden drone was discovered next to a Ukrainian cargo plane at Germany’s Leipzig airport, Poland has faced suspected acts of sabotage, and a string of unexplained explosions and fires have hit defence facilities supplying Ukraine across Europe. The attacks, aimed at sowing chaos and undermining support for Ukraine, vary widely in their ambition and sophistication, but share a common feature: they are often difficult to trace conclusively back to Moscow. That ambiguity is built into the way the operations are organised. Russian intelligence services have shifted away from relying primarily on professional operatives dispatched across Europe . Instead, suspected saboteurs are increasingly recruited remotely, including through Telegram channels, and paid in cryptocurrency to carry out individual tasks – allowing the Russian intelligence officers directing them to remain safely at home. The pattern was evident in Denmark this week, where authorities warned that Moscow was recruiting Danish citizens to carry out sabotage against defence companies with ties to Ukraine. But the growing scale of the attacks, and the speed with which European governments are now prepared to point the finger at Moscow, suggest the mood may be changing. When an incendiary parcel burst into flames at DHL’s Leipzig hub in July 2024 , it took about nine months before German investigators reported a concrete link to the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency. View image in fullscreen A police officer in protective clothing walks next to an explosive-disarming robot (EOD) at Leipzig airport after a drone was found near a runway last month. Photograph: Axel Schmidt/Reuters This time, Berlin moved far faster. Within days of the second incident at Leipzig airport, German officials publicly blamed Moscow – a sign both of growing confidence in identifying Russian operations and diminishing patience with what officials see as an increasingly brazen campaign of sabotage. Yet while Berlin has become quicker to point the finger at Moscow, its punishment for now has followed a more cautious path. Germany’s response to the failed Leipzig drone attack appeared calibrated to keep tensions in check, underscoring the harder question of what Europe can actually do beyond sanctions and diplomatic expulsions without risking a direct military confrontation. Berlin announced the closure of a Russian cultural centre and a Russian consulate, prompting Moscow to shut down the already gutted Goethe-Institut – a measured retaliation rather than a real escalation. Europe’s room for retaliation is also constrained by the powers given to its intelligence agencies. Unlike the CIA, many European services are primarily tasked with collecting intelligence and have far less latitude to conduct covert operations abroad. That leaves governments with relatively few tools between diplomatic and economic punishment on one end of the spectrum and overt military action on the other. To counter the shortcoming, several EU states, including the Netherlands, have recently put forward bills that would greatly expand the surveillance powers of the country’s intelligence agencies View image in fullscreen British armed forces intercept a Russian shadow fleet vessel in the Channel in June. Photograph: LPhot Hutchins/MoD Crown copyright/PA One area where Europe can point to more tangible action is its growing willingness to detain vessels linked to Russia’s shadow fleet . On Wednesday, Norwegian authorities seized a Russian vessel in the Arctic archipelago of Svalbard at Ukraine’s request. But critics argue that such measures are still not enough to deter Moscow. “Every time we do nothing, we invite Putin to continue,” said one EU lawmaker, speaking on condition of anonymity. That argument has been made most forcefully by Poland and the Baltic states, which have consistently pushed their western European allies to take a harder line against Moscow. “Hybrid war is not just a nuisance on the internet,” the Polish foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, said on Thursday. “Hybrid war means assassination squads, it means arsonists, it means blowing up moving trains, like in Poland, it means breaches of airspace with drones and cruise missiles.” “We need to convince Putin that such actions are not for free,” he added. At the same time, Sikorski also appeared to acknowledge, somewhat jokingly, the limits of Europe’s existing toolkit. Recalling Poland’s response to previous suspected Russian operations, he said: “Every time Russia committed arson or tried to blow up a moving train … I closed one Russian consulate, but I ran out of consulates to close.” Jakub Krupa contributed reporting Explore more on these topics Russia Ukraine Europe Germany Denmark Poland Norway analysis Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Shootout in Kyiv between Ukrainian spy services ‘disgraceful’, says Zelenskyy Germany blames Russia for drone attack at Leipzig airport Russian warship incident in Channel deeply concerning, says Starmer Russian airspace becoming unsafe for commercial airlines, Zelenskyy says Why did a Russian frigate fire warning shots and what can the UK do about it? https://idrw.org/india-in-touch-with-rus.text: India has been in continuous touch with both the Ukrainian and Russian sides and is trying to see if there are ideas and suggestions which can be developed in some way that will contribute to the mitigation or the cessation of the conflict, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said on Friday. Jaishankar, who arrived in Warsaw from Kyiv where he held talks with top Ukrainian leadership on Thursday, made the remarks after he met Poland’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosaw Sikorski. Addressing a joint press meet alongside Sikorski, Jaishankar said that he discussed the complex global challenges, including supply chain resilience and food, fuel and fertiliser security, with his Polish counterpart. “The Deputy Prime Minister and I also understandably discussed some major global and regional issues, notable among them is the war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year… I myself have just come here from Kyiv,” he said, referring to his visit to Ukraine a day earlier. Replying to a question, he said India has been in continuous touch with both the Ukrainian and Russian sides. “What we are trying to do is to see if there are ideas and suggestions which can be developed in some way in which they will contribute to the mitigation, ideally, the cessation of the conflict,” he added. A day earlier, Jaishankar had said in Ukraine that India is ready to extend “any help in any manner” to end the Ukraine-Russia war. He had met President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Sybiha in Kyiv on Thursday. After talks with Jaishankar, Zelenskyy had said that he was “grateful to India for its commitment to ending this unjust war.” “This certainly must not be a time of war. Peace is needed. This is India’s clear position,” he said and hoped that other major world powers would also take a clear stance that this war must end and that a reliable peace must be achieved. On Friday, Jaishankar reiterated that India believes that endless war must give way to an end to war. “These are wars without winners. Every additional day means more death, more destruction, more loss to the parties themselves, and more cost to the rest of the world,” he said in Warsaw. He recalled that this concern was voiced publicly by Prime Minister Narendra Modi recently. “Our efforts must therefore focus on promoting dialogue and diplomacy. We must each do what we can in whichever way we believe could be most effective and support the efforts of others to bring this conflict to an end. This is India’s strong conviction, and we are acting on it,” he added. On India’s purchases of Russian oil, the minister said the issue is a conflict, and its solution lies in negotiations, not in trade.”This war is not going to end… not because somebody chose to buy or not buy oil or alumina or fertilisers or metals and minerals. It will end when there is diplomacy, when there is dialogue and when there is negotiation. So, I think let’s diagnose the problem right,” he said while replying to another question.

Moneycontrol World Desk October 03, 2026 / 15:15 IST Latvia votes in a parliamentary election shaped by drone incursions, the war in Ukraine and concerns over Russia. Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs is seeking a full term after taking office in May. (Image: AFP) Latvians vote in an election focused on security. PM Kulbergs seeks full term after taking office in May. Cost of living and economy also key election issues. Did our AI summary help? Market Mastery Webinar by Vishal Malkan Find the weak links in your portfolio by Vishal Malkan Register for FREE Webinar Register for FREE Latvians voted Saturday to elect a new parliament in an election shaped by security concerns, repeated drone incursions and the war in neighbouring Ukraine, with Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs seeking a full term after taking office in May. Kulbergs came to power after the previous coalition collapsed over its handling of incidents involving stray military drones that entered Latvian airspace. The drones were Ukrainian, although Latvian officials have blamed Russia's war against Ukraine for causing them to divert from their flight paths. Parliament subsequently approved a four-party coalition led by Kulbergs ahead of the election. Russia, Ukraine and Latvia's security concerns Latvia, a NATO and European Union member, borders Russia and Belarus and has strongly backed Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion. Security concerns have been central to the campaign, with Baltic officials warning about Russian sabotage, cyberattacks and other forms of hybrid activity. Russia has rejected such accusations, while Western officials have said Moscow is not assessed as capable of launching a direct assault on NATO. NATO also strengthened protection of Latvian airspace during the election period, with Germany deploying four Eurofighter jets to Latvia for about a week. Latvia's State Security Service said it had not detected any significant or systematic attempts by Russia or other actors to influence the election in favour of a particular party or candidate. Related Stories Putin says Russia’s ‘security zone’ inside Ukraine will be non-negotiable in peace talks Ukraine runs out of Patriot interceptors as Zelenskyy’s ties with Trump come under strain Russian officer secretly fed Ukraine battle plans, helped kill 300 soldiers before dramatic escape: ... Kulbergs has campaigned on continued support for Ukraine, stronger anti-drone capabilities and maintaining defence spending at 5% of gross domestic product. Cost of living adds to security debate While security remains a major concern, cost-of-living pressures, wages, healthcare and the economy have also featured prominently in the campaign. Opinion polls put Kulbergs' United List ahead at around 14%, while several other parties were within reach of the 5% threshold required to enter parliament. A September 4–16 SKDS/LSM poll cited by Reuters found seven of the 14 parties could cross the threshold, while around one-third of respondents were undecided or did not intend to vote. Sovereign Power has opposed military aid to Ukraine and argued that more government resources should be directed towards domestic concerns. Party leader Julia Stepanenko told Reuters that its voters want an end to air alerts and for the war to be resolved through peace talks. The Progressives, meanwhile, support Ukraine and have a left-leaning platform. Fourteen party lists are contesting the election for Latvia's 100-member Saeima, which serves four-year terms. Parties must receive at least 5% of the vote to win parliamentary seats, with the fragmented political landscape making coalition talks an important part of the government-formation process after the results.
